apis.name: GetSystemInfo
apis.summary: Retrieves information about the current system, including processor architecture, processor count, page size, and address limits.
apis.description: GetSystemInfo fills a SYSTEM_INFO structure with information about the current system as seen by the calling process. The structure reports the processor architecture, the number of logical processors in the current processor group, page size, allocation granularity, processor affinity mask, and the minimum and maximum application addresses. The values are commonly used to size memory allocations and to adapt to the host architecture. The function returns no value and reports no error through GetLastError.

parameters.name: lpSystemInfo
parameters.description: A pointer to a SYSTEM_INFO structure that receives the system information. The pointer must be valid; the function does not accept NULL.

return.success: The function fills lpSystemInfo with system information and returns no value.
return.failure: There is no return value or documented error path; pass a valid SYSTEM_INFO pointer.

apis.remarks: dwPageSize and dwAllocationGranularity are distinct values and should not be used interchangeably when planning virtual memory. dwNumberOfProcessors reports the logical processor count for the current processor group, which can differ from the total on systems with multiple groups. On WOW64, use GetNativeSystemInfo when the native architecture is required.
apis.maldev_notes: System information queries are pervasive in ordinary software, including installers, runtimes, and management agents. Analysis may encounter them in environment checks, but the call is benign in isolation and becomes interesting only in the context of how the results influence behavior.
apis.defensive_notes: Environment discovery is high-volume and usually legitimate. Sequences that combine architecture, processor count, and memory limits with other host checks can be relevant context, but no single system-information call is a detection.

example.title: Read page size and allocation granularity
example.notes: The example fills a zero-initialized SYSTEM_INFO structure and performs a basic sanity check. It requires no privileges and is illustrative only.

apis.source_notes: Void return, SYSTEM_INFO fields, and WOW64 guidance checked against Microsoft Learn (sysinfoapi.h).

apis.name: GetNativeSystemInfo
apis.summary: Retrieves information about the native system, including when the caller is running under WOW64.
apis.description: GetNativeSystemInfo fills a SYSTEM_INFO structure using the native system's architecture and limits. It is intended for 32-bit processes running under WOW64 that need information about the 64-bit host rather than the emulated environment. When called from a 64-bit process, its behavior is equivalent to GetSystemInfo. Like GetSystemInfo, it returns no value and does not report errors through GetLastError.

parameters.name: lpSystemInfo
parameters.description: A pointer to a SYSTEM_INFO structure that receives the native system information. The pointer must be valid; the function does not accept NULL.

return.success: The function fills lpSystemInfo with native system information and returns no value.
return.failure: There is no return value or documented error path; pass a valid SYSTEM_INFO pointer.

apis.remarks: Use this function when a 32-bit process needs the native processor architecture or address limits. A 64-bit process can call either function, and the results are equivalent. The structure's processor architecture field reflects the native system rather than the WOW64 emulation.
apis.maldev_notes: WOW64-aware environment queries appear in legitimate software that must adapt to the host architecture. In analysis they can indicate awareness of the process's bitness and the underlying system, but the call itself is ordinary.
apis.defensive_notes: Comparing GetSystemInfo and GetNativeSystemInfo results can help explain whether a process is running under WOW64. The distinction is architectural, not behavioral evidence of malicious intent.
apis.source_notes: WOW64 behavior and equivalence to GetSystemInfo on 64-bit processes checked against Microsoft Learn (sysinfoapi.h).

apis.name: GetComputerNameW
apis.summary: Retrieves the NetBIOS name of the local computer.
apis.description: GetComputerNameW copies the computer's NetBIOS name into a caller-supplied buffer. The name is established at system startup and does not include a domain suffix. The size parameter is expressed in characters: on input it gives the buffer capacity, and on output it receives the number of characters copied, excluding the terminating null. If the buffer is too small, the function fails with ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW and the size parameter receives the required capacity. For DNS host names and other formats, use GetComputerNameExW.

parameters.name: lpBuffer
parameters.description: A buffer that receives the null-terminated computer name. The buffer should hold at least MAX_COMPUTERNAME_LENGTH + 1 characters.

parameters.name: nSize
parameters.description: On input, the size of lpBuffer in characters, including room for the terminating null. On success, receives the number of characters copied, excluding the null. If the buffer is too small, receives the required buffer size, including the terminating null.

return.success: A nonzero value; lpBuffer contains the null-terminated computer name and nSize holds the character count excluding the null.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError; ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW indicates that the buffer was too small.

apis.remarks: MAX_COMPUTERNAME_LENGTH is 15, so a 16-character buffer is sufficient for the NetBIOS name plus its terminator. The returned name is not the fully qualified DNS name. Renaming the computer requires a restart before the new name is reported by this function.
apis.maldev_notes: Host names are routinely collected by installers, management agents, telemetry, and diagnostics. In sample analysis, host and user queries may precede configuration or targeting decisions, but they are equally common in legitimate software and are not evidence by themselves.
apis.defensive_notes: Hostname collection is high-volume benign behavior. It is more useful to consider what other data is gathered and where it is sent than to flag the query alone.

example.title: Read the local NetBIOS computer name
example.notes: The example sizes the buffer for the documented NetBIOS limit and checks the return value. No privileges are required, and the snippet is illustrative only.

apis.source_notes: Buffer sizing, character-count semantics, and ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW behavior checked against Microsoft Learn (winbase.h).

apis.name: GetUserNameW
apis.summary: Retrieves the name of the user associated with the calling thread.
apis.description: GetUserNameW returns the account name of the user associated with the calling thread. If the thread is impersonating another client, the returned name is the impersonated client's name rather than the process owner's name. The buffer size is expressed in characters and includes the terminating null. When the buffer is too small, the function fails with ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER and the size parameter receives the required size, including the null. For domain-qualified or alternate formats, use GetUserNameExW.

parameters.name: lpBuffer
parameters.description: A buffer that receives the null-terminated user name. A buffer of UNLEN + 1 characters is typically sufficient.

parameters.name: pcbBuffer
parameters.description: On input, the size of lpBuffer in characters. On success, receives the number of characters copied, including the terminating null. If the buffer is too small, receives the required size including the null.

return.success: A nonzero value; lpBuffer contains the null-terminated user name and pcbBuffer holds the size including the null.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError; ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER indicates that the buffer was too small.

apis.remarks: UNLEN is defined as 256, so a buffer of UNLEN + 1 characters is typically sufficient; include lmcons.h when using UNLEN. The returned name is not necessarily domain-qualified. Because the function follows the thread's impersonation state, the result can differ from the identity of the process that created the thread.
apis.maldev_notes: User identity queries are common in installers, management software, and diagnostics. In analysis, a user name can help establish the token or impersonation context, but querying it is not inherently suspicious.
apis.defensive_notes: User names are widely logged and rarely distinctive. When impersonation is in use, compare the returned name with the process token and thread token to avoid misattributing activity.
apis.source_notes: Impersonation behavior, buffer-size semantics, and ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER handling checked against Microsoft Learn (winbase.h).

apis.name: IsDebuggerPresent
apis.summary: Determines whether the calling process is being debugged by a user-mode debugger.
apis.description: IsDebuggerPresent reports whether a user-mode debugger is attached to the calling process. It examines only the caller; it cannot inspect another process. The function returns a nonzero value when the process is being debugged and zero otherwise, and it does not use GetLastError to report failure. The check is common in diagnostics, crash-reporting code, and analysis-aware software that changes behavior when a debugger is attached.

return.success: A nonzero value if the calling process is being debugged by a user-mode debugger.
return.failure: Zero if the process is not being debugged by a user-mode debugger. The function does not report errors through GetLastError.

apis.remarks: The check is limited to the calling process and to user-mode debuggers. Kernel-mode debuggers and other instrumentation are outside its scope, so a zero result does not prove that no analysis tooling is present. The result reflects the process's debug state at the time of the call.
apis.maldev_notes: Debugger checks appear in both benign diagnostics and analysis-aware code. In sample analysis, a call indicates that the program may branch on debugger state; it is one signal and can be affected by legitimate debuggers, debugger configuration, and instrumentation, so the result should be corroborated with other evidence.
apis.defensive_notes: A debugger check is not inherently malicious. Analysts can note where the result influences control flow and combine it with other behavior; ordinary debuggers and crash tooling can change the result.
apis.source_notes: User-mode scope, zero-parameter prototype, and return convention checked against Microsoft Learn (debugapi.h).

apis.name: CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent
apis.summary: Determines whether a specified process is being debugged.
apis.description: CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent queries the debug state of a process identified by a handle and stores the result in a BOOL. Unlike IsDebuggerPresent, it can examine another process, subject to the access permitted by the handle. The function returns nonzero when the query itself succeeds; the debug state is reported separately through pbDebuggerPresent, which is set to TRUE or FALSE. A zero return therefore means the query failed, not that no debugger is attached.

parameters.name: hProcess
parameters.description: A handle to the process to query. The handle must permit process query operations; OpenProcess with query access is the usual way to obtain it.

parameters.name: pbDebuggerPresent
parameters.description: A pointer to a BOOL that receives TRUE if the process is being debugged and FALSE otherwise. The pointer must be valid.

return.success: A nonzero value; pbDebuggerPresent contains the debug state of the target process.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError. Do not interpret a zero return as meaning that the process is not being debugged.

apis.remarks: The target handle must remain valid for the duration of the call. The result reflects the target's debug state at that moment and may be affected by the type of debugger, the process state, and the permissions of the caller. Always test the return value before reading pbDebuggerPresent.
apis.maldev_notes: Remote debugger checks are used by debuggers, crash handlers, and analysis-aware software. A positive result is one signal and can be caused by legitimate debugging or instrumentation; it should be corroborated rather than treated as conclusive.
apis.defensive_notes: Querying another process's debug state can be relevant when combined with cross-process handle access, but monitoring and debugging tools do this routinely. Interpret the access mask and the caller's role together.
apis.source_notes: Separate return-value and output-parameter semantics checked against Microsoft Learn (debugapi.h).

apis.summary: Retrieves the load address for each device driver in the system.
apis.description: Retrieves the load address for each device driver in the system.
apis.prototype: BOOL EnumDeviceDrivers(LPVOID* lpImageBase, DWORD cb, LPDWORD lpcbNeeded);

parameters.name: lpImageBase
parameters.description: An array that receives the list of load addresses for the device drivers.

parameters.name: cb
parameters.description: The size of the lpImageBase array, in bytes. If the array is not large enough to store the load addresses, the lpcbNeeded parameter receives the required size of the array.

parameters.description: The number of bytes returned in the lpImageBase array.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: To determine how many device drivers were enumerated by the call to EnumDeviceDrivers, divide the resulting value in the lpcbNeeded parameter by sizeof(LPVOID). Starting with Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2, Psapi.h establishes version numbers for the PSAPI functions. The PSAPI version number affects the name used to call the function and the library that a program must load. If PSAPI_VERSION is 2 or greater, this function is defined as K32EnumDeviceDrivers in Psapi.h and exported in Kernel32.lib and Kernel32.dll. If PSAPI_VERSION is 1, this function is defined as EnumDeviceDrivers in Psapi.h and exported in Psapi.lib and Psapi.dll as a wrapper that calls K32EnumDeviceDrivers. Programs that must run on earlier versions of Windows as well as Windows 7 and later versions should always call this function as EnumDeviceDrivers. To ensure correct resolution of symbols, add Psapi.lib to the TARGETLIBS macro and compile the program with –DPSAPI_VERSION=1. To use run-time dynamic linking, load Psapi.dll. Starting in Windows 11 Version 24H2, EnumDeviceDrivers will require SeDebugPrivilege to return valid ImageBase values. The function will still succeed if the caller does not have this privilege enabled, but the returned lpImageBase array will contain addresses that are all NULL. #### Examples For an example, see Enumerating all Device Drivers in the System.

apis.description: Enumerates the locales that are either installed on or supported by an operating system. Note For interoperability reasons, the application should prefer the EnumSystemLocalesEx function to EnumSystemLocales because Microsoft is migrating toward the use of locale names instead of locale identifiers for new locales. Any application that will be run only on Windows Vista and later should use EnumSystemLocalesEx.

parameters.name: lpLocaleEnumProc
parameters.description: Pointer to an application-defined callback function. For more information, see EnumLocalesProc.

parameters.name: dwFlags
parameters.description: Flags specifying the locale identifiers to enumerate. The flags can be used singly or combined using a binary OR. If the application specifies 0 for this parameter, the function behaves as for LCID_SUPPORTED. Value Meaning LCID_INSTALLED Enumerate only installed locale identifiers. This value cannot be used with LCID_SUPPORTED. LCID_SUPPORTED Enumerate all supported locale identifiers. This value cannot be used with LCID_INSTALLED. LCID_ALTERNATE_SORTS Enumerate only the alternate sort locale identifiers. If this value is used with either LCID_INSTALLED or LCID_SUPPORTED, the installed or supported locales are retrieved, as well as the alternate sort locale identifiers.

return.success: Returns a nonzero value if successful, or 0 otherwise. To get extended error information, the application can call GetLastError, which can return one of the following error codes:
return.failure: ERROR_BADDB. The function could not access the data. This situation should not normally occur, and typically indicates a bad installation, a disk problem, or the like. ERROR_INVALID_FLAGS. The values supplied for flags were not valid. ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER. Any of the parameter values was invalid.

apis.remarks: The function enumerates locales by passing locale identifiers, one at a time, to the specified application-defined callback function. This continues until all of the installed or supported locale identifiers have been passed to the callback function or the callback function returns FALSE. > > The winnls.h header defines EnumSystemLocales as an alias that automatically selects the ANSI or Unicode version of this function based on the definition of the UNICODE preprocessor constant. Mixing usage of the encoding-neutral alias with code that is not encoding-neutral can lead to mismatches that result in compilation or runtime errors. For more information, see Conventions for Function Prototypes.

apis.summary: Retrieves information about logical processors and related hardware.
apis.description: Retrieves information about logical processors and related hardware. To retrieve information about logical processors and related hardware, including processor groups, use the GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx function.

Your application can use this information when affinitizing your threads and processes to take best advantage of the hardware properties of the platform, or to determine the number of logical and physical processors for licensing purposes. Applications calling this function must be prepared to handle additional indicator values in the future. Note that the order in which the structures are returned in the buffer may change between calls to this function. The size of the SYSTEM_LOGICAL_PROCESSOR_INFORMATION structure varies between processor architectures and versions of Windows. apis.name: GetTickCount
apis.summary: Retrieves the number of milliseconds that have elapsed since the system was started, up to 49.7 days.
apis.description: Retrieves the number of milliseconds that have elapsed since the system was started, up to 49.7 days.

return.success: The return value is the number of milliseconds that have elapsed since the system was started.

apis.remarks: The resolution of the GetTickCount function is limited to the resolution of the system timer, which is typically in the range of 10 milliseconds to 16 milliseconds. The resolution of the GetTickCount function is not affected by adjustments made by the GetSystemTimeAdjustment function. The elapsed time is stored as a DWORD value. Therefore, the time will wrap around to zero if the system is run continuously for 49.7 days. To avoid this problem, use the GetTickCount64 function. Otherwise, check for an overflow condition when comparing times. If you need a higher resolution timer, use a multimedia timer or a high-resolution timer. To obtain the time elapsed since the computer was started, retrieve the System Up Time counter in the performance data in the registry key HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA. The value returned is an 8-byte value. For more information, see Performance Counters. To obtain the time the system has spent in the working state since it was started, use the QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime function. Note The QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime function produces different results on debug ("checked") builds of Windows, because the interrupt-time count and tick count are advanced by approximately 49 days. This helps to identify bugs that might not occur until the system has been running for a long time.

apis.name: TimeGetTime
apis.summary: The timeGetTime function retrieves the system time, in milliseconds.
apis.description: The timeGetTime function retrieves the system time, in milliseconds. The system time is the time elapsed since Windows was started.

return.success: Returns the system time, in milliseconds.

apis.remarks: The only difference between this function and the timeGetSystemTime function is that timeGetSystemTime uses the MMTIME structure to return the system time. The timeGetTime function has less overhead than timeGetSystemTime. Note that the value returned by the timeGetTime function is a DWORD value. The return value wraps around to 0 every 2^32 milliseconds, which is about 49.71 days. This can cause problems in code that directly uses the timeGetTime return value in computations, particularly where the value is used to control code execution. You should always use the difference between two timeGetTime return values in computations. The default precision of the timeGetTime function can be five milliseconds or more, depending on the machine. You can use the timeBeginPeriod and timeEndPeriod functions to increase the precision of timeGetTime. If you do so, the minimum difference between successive values returned by timeGetTime can be as large as the minimum period value set using timeBeginPeriod and timeEndPeriod. Use the QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency functions to measure short time intervals at a high resolution.
